questions.question: How do you declare and initialize an array in Java, and what are the default values?
questions.title: Array Declaration and Initialization in Java
questions.direct_answer: An array in Java is declared with a type followed by `[]` and a name, then initialized using `new type[size]` or with a literal `{val1, val2, ...}`. Until you assign values, Java fills the array with defaults: `0` for numbers, `false` for booleans, `null` for objects.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the three declaration styles, understand how Java allocates array memory on the heap, and know that arrays have fixed size and auto-filled default values.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing the declaration `int[] arr` (no memory yet) with initialization `new int[5]` (memory allocated). Also assuming elements are random garbage values — Java always zero-fills.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that the array reference lives on the stack while the actual block of elements lives on the heap — and that `arr.length` is a field, not a method, so no parentheses.

sections.title: The One Line That Secretly Does Two Different Things
sections.content:
An array is a **fixed-size container** that holds many values of the same type, lined up one after another. If you have five test scores, instead of five separate variables you keep them all in one `int[]` and reach each value by its position number.

That position number is called the **index**, and Java counts from `0`. So a five-element array has slots `0, 1, 2, 3, 4`.

Creating an array is really two steps, even when you write them on one line. `int[] scores` makes a **reference variable** — a small named slot on the stack that will hold the address of an array, but points to nothing yet. `new int[5]` does the real work: Java goes to the **heap** (the region of memory where objects live), reserves five `int`-sized slots sitting next to each other, and hands back their address. The `=` copies that address into `scores`. Only now does an actual array exist.

Here is the part beginners coming from C find surprising: Java fills those slots for you, never with garbage. Numbers start at `0`, `boolean` at `false`, and object types like `String` at `null` — guaranteed by the language spec, not luck.

Two details interviewers listen for. There are three ways to initialize: `new int[5]` to fill later, the literal `{1, 2, 3}` when you already have the values, and `new int[]{1, 2, 3}` to build one inline. And `arr.length` is a field, not a method, so it takes no parentheses.

The gotcha: once an array is five wide, it is five forever. Arrays cannot grow or shrink — and that single limitation is the whole reason `ArrayList` exists.

sections.title: What Happens in Memory When You Write `int[] scores = new int[5]`
sections.content:
The reference lives on the stack; the actual data block lives on the heap. They are two separate things connected by an address. ```mermaid flowchart LR Stack["Stack
──────
scores
@ 0xFF10"] -->|"points to"| Heap["Heap
──────────────────
[0] = 0
[1] = 0
[2] = 0
[3] = 0
[4] = 0
(size fixed at 5)"] ``` `scores` is just the address. The five `int` slots are the real thing — they live on the heap and are zero-filled until you put something in them.

sections.title: Three Ways to Declare and Initialize — Plus Default Values in Action
Default Values by Element Type
sections.content:
| Array element type | Default value | Example declaration |
|---|---|---|
| `byte`, `short`, `int`, `long` | `0` | `int[] arr = new int[5]` |
| `float`, `double` | `0.0` | `double[] arr = new double[3]` |
| `boolean` | `false` | `boolean[] flags = new boolean[4]` |
| `char` | `'\u0000'` (null char) | `char[] chars = new char[3]` |
| Any object (`String`, `Object`, etc.) | `null` | `String[] names = new String[3]` |

sections.title: When a Plain Array Is the Right Call
sections.content:
**Reach for a plain array** when the size is known and fixed the moment you create it — a 7-day week, the three RGB channels of a pixel, a chessboard's `8x8` grid. The fixed size is a feature here: it documents your intent, and the JVM lays the elements out in one tight, contiguous memory block, so indexed access is about as fast as Java gets.

**Which initialization style you pick depends on what you know:**

- Use the literal `{1, 2, 3}` when you already have the values in hand
- Use `new int[n]` when you know only the count and will fill the slots in a loop
- Prefer `new type[]{...}` when you want to build a fresh array inline and pass it straight into a method call

The moment the count is unknown or changes as the program runs — reading lines from a file, collecting user clicks — **stop fighting the fixed size and switch to `ArrayList`**. Manually copying into a bigger array every time you outgrow the old one is exactly the work `ArrayList` was created to do for you.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Writing `arr.length()`** — `length` is a field on an array, not a method, so the parentheses are a compile error. Only `String` uses `length()`; arrays use `arr.length`.
- **Expecting garbage values** — beginners coming from C sometimes add code to "clear" a new array first. Java already zero-fills every slot (`0`, `false`, `null`), so that work is wasted.
- **Indexing an array you only declared** — a field left as `int[] arr;` is `null`, and `arr[0] = 1` throws `NullPointerException`, not an empty-array error. You must assign with `new` (or a literal) before indexing.
- **Reading index `length`** — a 5-element array's last valid index is `4`; `arr[arr.length]` always throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` because indices run `0` to `length - 1`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Two-step reality**: `int[] arr` declares a null reference on the stack; `new int[5]` allocates the actual block on the heap.
- **Fixed size**: once created with `new int[5]`, the array is always 5 elements — you cannot resize it.
- **Auto zero-fill**: Java fills every slot with a type-appropriate default — `0`, `false`, or `null` — never random garbage.
- **`arr.length` not `arr.length()`**: length is a field on the array object, not a method — no parentheses.
- **Index starts at 0**: valid indices are `0` to `arr.length - 1`; going beyond throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
I'd point out that a line like `int[] scores = new int[5]` is really **doing two separate jobs**. The `int[] scores` part creates a reference variable on the stack, and right then it points to nothing. The `new int[5]` part is what actually reserves five slots on the heap and hands back their address, which the equals sign stores in the variable — only at that moment does a real array exist.

There are **three ways to initialize**:

- `new int[5]` when you'll fill it in a loop
- the literal `{1, 2, 3}` when you already have the values
- `new int[]{1, 2, 3}` when you want to build one inline for a method call

The detail I'd be sure to mention is that **Java zero-fills every slot automatically** — `0`, `false`, or `null`, never garbage — so you never read random data from a fresh array. And it's `arr.length`, **a field with no parentheses**, unlike `String`'s `length()` method.

The thing I'd close on is that **the size is locked the instant you create it** — the day you need it to grow is the day you reach for an `ArrayList`.

questions.question: What is ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and how do you prevent it?
questions.title: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException in Java
questions.direct_answer: `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` is a `RuntimeException` thrown when you try to access an array index that does not exist — either negative or equal to/greater than `array.length`. It is prevented by always looping with `i < arr.length` and checking bounds before direct access.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand valid array index range and can identify the classic off-by-one mistake in a loop.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing `i <= arr.length` instead of `i < arr.length` in a for loop — this is the most common cause by far.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that it is an unchecked RuntimeException (extends IndexOutOfBoundsException → RuntimeException), so the compiler never warns you — only happens at runtime.

sections.title: Why Asking for the Sixth Slot of a Five-Slot Array Crashes
sections.content:
Every element in an array has a position number, and in Java those numbers start at `0`. That position is called the **index** — the first element is `arr[0]`, the second is `arr[1]`, and so on.

This is where one of the most common beginner crashes comes from: **the indices run from `0` to `length − 1`, not `1` to `length`**. A five-element array has slots `0, 1, 2, 3, 4`. There is no slot `5`.

When you ask for a slot that does not exist — `arr[5]` on that array — Java checks the index against the array's length while the program runs, sees it is out of range, and throws **`ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`**. Think of it as Java refusing to read past the end of the block rather than handing you whatever random memory happens to sit there, which is what C would do.

Why doesn't the compiler catch this for you? Because **the index is almost always a variable** — `arr[i]`, where `i` is worked out while the program runs. The compiler has no way to know what `i` will be, so the check has to happen live, on every single access.

One nuance worth saying out loud: this is an **unchecked** `RuntimeException`. Nothing forces you to wrap it in a try-catch; the code compiles cleanly and simply crashes the moment it fires.

The classic gotcha is a loop written `i <= arr.length` instead of `i < arr.length`. **That one extra `=` lets `i` reach `5`**, and `arr[5]` blows up. A negative index like `arr[-1]` throws too — unlike Python, Java has no notion of counting back from the end.

sections.title: Valid Index Range for a 5-Element Array
sections.content:
Valid indices are always 0 to length−1. One step beyond either end throws the exception. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["access arr[i]"] --> B{"i >= 0 AND
i < arr.length?"} B -->|"yes"| C["access element
— safe"] B -->|"no"| D["ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
thrown at runtime"] ``` For `int[] arr = new int[5]`: valid is 0–4. Trying `arr[5]` or `arr[-1]` both trigger the exception.

sections.title: The Classic Off-By-One Mistake — and the Fix
Picking the Loop That Can't Go Out of Bounds
sections.content:
**When you only need to read each element** and don't care about its position, use the enhanced for loop — `for (int x : arr)`. There is no index to mismanage, so it physically cannot throw `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. Make this your default for read-only traversal.

**Reach for a classic indexed `for` loop** only when you actually need the index:

- to write back into the array
- to compare neighbouring elements
- to step by more than one

There, always write `i < arr.length`, never `<=`, and never hardcode the upper bound.

When you access a single element from a variable index — say, a number that came from user input or a calculation — guard it with `if (i >= 0 && i < arr.length)` before you touch the array. The rule that keeps you safe is simple: **validate the index first, index second**.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`i <= arr.length` in a loop** — the extra `=` runs one more iteration and reads `arr[length]`, which never exists. This single typo causes the large majority of these crashes.
- **Assuming negative indexing works** — `arr[-1]` does not mean "last element" like in Python; it throws immediately. The last element is `arr[arr.length - 1]`.
- **Hardcoding an index** — `arr[10]` on an array that might hold three elements crashes; guard any variable index with a bounds check first.
- **Catching it instead of fixing it** — wrapping the access in try-catch hides the off-by-one rather than correcting the loop. The bug is the index logic, not a recoverable runtime condition.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Valid range is `0` to `arr.length - 1`** — a 5-element array has no element at index 5.
- **Off-by-one in loops**: `i <= arr.length` is the #1 cause — always use `i < arr.length`.
- **Use enhanced for when you don't need the index**: `for (int x : arr)` is guaranteed safe.
- **Unchecked exception**: extends `RuntimeException` — the compiler never warns you; it crashes at runtime.
- **Negative indices also throw it**: unlike Python, Java has no concept of `arr[-1]` for last element — use `arr[arr.length - 1]`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The crash everyone hits on the very last loop iteration is the way into this one. **Array indices in Java start at zero**, so a five-element array's last valid index is four, not five — and `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` is what you get the moment you reach outside that `0` to `length − 1` range.

The compiler can't catch it because the index is usually a variable that's only known at runtime, and it's an **unchecked `RuntimeException`**, so nothing forces you to handle it — it just crashes when it fires. **By far the most common cause** is a loop written `i <= arr.length` instead of strictly less-than, which runs one iteration too many.

So I always loop with `i < arr.length`, and when I only need to read the values I reach for the **enhanced for loop**, since with no index there's nothing to get wrong. For a single lookup from a variable, I guard it with a bounds check first.

And unlike Python, **Java has no negative indexing** — the last element is `arr[arr.length − 1]`, never `arr[-1]`.

questions.question: What is the difference between an array and an ArrayList in Java?
questions.title: Array vs ArrayList in Java
questions.direct_answer: An array has a fixed size set at creation and can hold primitives directly. An `ArrayList` is a resizable list backed by an array internally — it grows automatically, supports only objects (not primitives), and offers utility methods like `add()`, `remove()`, and `contains()`. Use arrays when size is known and performance matters; use `ArrayList` when you need dynamic sizing.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the fixed-size constraint of arrays vs dynamic resizing of ArrayList, and know when to choose one over the other.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying ArrayList is always better — arrays are faster for indexed access and are the right tool when the size is known upfront (e.g. a 12-month calendar, a 3-channel RGB value).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that ArrayList internally uses an array and doubles its capacity when full — so it is not magic, just an array with automatic resize logic wrapped around it.

sections.title: The Real Question Isn't Which Is Better — It's Whether the Size Changes
sections.content:
An array and an `ArrayList` both hold a sequence of values that you reach by position. **The one difference that drives everything else** is simple: an array's size is fixed the moment you create it, while an `ArrayList` grows and shrinks as you go.

Why does `ArrayList` exist at all? Because **real programs often don't know up front how many items they'll have**. An array fixes its size at birth — `int[] scores = new int[5]` reserves exactly five slots, permanently. Need a sixth? You'd have to allocate a bigger array and copy everything across by hand. There is no `add()`.

`ArrayList` takes that chore off your hands. `ArrayList<Integer> scores = new ArrayList<>()` starts with room for a few elements and **grows itself** when you exceed that. The mechanism is not magic: internally it holds a plain array, and when that array fills, it allocates a new one about **1.5× larger** (the formula is `oldCapacity + oldCapacity >> 1`), copies the elements over, and swaps it in. You just call `add()` and never see it happen.

That convenience costs two things, and interviewers listen for them:

- `ArrayList` stores **objects only**, so an `int` becomes a boxed `Integer` with a little memory and speed overhead — you cannot write `ArrayList<int>`
- you read elements with `get(i)` instead of raw `[]`, and ask its length with `size()` (a method) instead of `length` (a field)

The gotcha to avoid is the reflex answer that "`ArrayList` is just better." It isn't — for a known, fixed count of primitives, like a 12-month total or an RGB triple, an array is smaller and faster. So the rule is concrete: **fixed count and primitives, use an array; a count that changes at runtime, use an `ArrayList`**.

sections.title: Array vs ArrayList — Side by Side
sections.content:
| Feature | Array | ArrayList |
|---|---|---|
| Size | Fixed at creation — cannot change | Dynamic — grows automatically |
| Syntax | `int[] arr = new int[5]` | `ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>()` |
| Primitives | Supports `int`, `double`, etc. directly | Objects only — `int` must be `Integer` |
| Access | `arr[0]` | `list.get(0)` |
| Add element | Not possible (fixed) | `list.add(value)` |
| Remove element | Not possible (fixed) | `list.remove(index)` |
| Length / size | `arr.length` (field) | `list.size()` (method) |
| Performance | Faster — direct memory block | Slightly slower — object + boxing overhead |
| Use when | Size known upfront, primitives needed | Size changes at runtime, need add/remove |

sections.title: Same Task — Array vs ArrayList
Which One to Choose?
sections.content:
A simple decision tree for picking between array and ArrayList: ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Need to store a sequence"] --> B{"Is the size fixed
and known upfront?"} B -->|"Yes"| C{"Need primitives
int, double, etc.?"} C -->|"Yes"| D["Use array
int[] arr = new int[n]"] C -->|"No"| E["Array or ArrayList
both work"] B -->|"No — size
changes at runtime"| F["Use ArrayList
list.add() / list.remove()"] ```

sections.title: Choosing Between Them in Practice
sections.content:
**Default to an array** when the size is genuinely fixed and known up front — a 12-month total, a fixed-size buffer, the `8x8` of a chessboard — or when you're storing large volumes of primitives and want to avoid boxing overhead. Arrays are also the natural choice in tight numeric loops where every nanosecond of raw indexed access counts.

**Default to `ArrayList`** for almost everything else, especially when you don't know how many elements you'll end up with:

- reading rows from a database
- accumulating events
- building a result whose length depends on the input

The convenience of `add()`, `remove()`, and `contains()` plus automatic growth outweighs the small overhead in the vast majority of application code.

A useful tell: if you find yourself manually tracking a `count` variable alongside an array and reallocating a bigger one whenever it fills, **you've reinvented `ArrayList` by hand** — just use it.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Mixing up `length` and `size()`** — arrays use the field `arr.length`; `ArrayList` uses the method `list.size()`. Calling `arr.size()` or `list.length` is a compile error and a classic exam trap.
- **Trying `ArrayList<int>`** — generics only accept reference types, so it must be `ArrayList<Integer>`. Autoboxing converts the `int`, but storing millions of boxed `Integer`s costs far more memory than an `int[]`.
- **Array covariance bites at runtime** — `Object[] arr = new String[3]; arr[0] = 42;` compiles fine but throws `ArrayStoreException` at runtime, because the real array is a `String[]`. Generics close this hole: a `List<String>` simply won't let you add an `Integer` at compile time.
- **`list.remove(2)` on an `ArrayList<Integer>`** — this removes the element at *index* 2, not the value `2`. To delete the value you must call `list.remove(Integer.valueOf(2))`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Fixed vs dynamic**: arrays are fixed-size forever; `ArrayList` resizes itself by allocating a new internal array about 1.5× larger and copying over.
- **Primitives vs objects**: arrays support `int`, `double`, etc. directly; `ArrayList` needs wrapper types (`Integer`, `Double`).
- **API richness**: `ArrayList` gives you `add()`, `remove()`, `contains()`, `indexOf()` — arrays give you nothing but `[]` access.
- **`length` vs `size()`**: arrays use `arr.length` (field); `ArrayList` uses `list.size()` (method) — mixing these up is a common mistake.
- **Under the hood**: `ArrayList` is just an array with auto-resize logic — indexed access (`get(i)`) is still O(1).

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
I'd frame it as **one decision: does the number of elements change while the program runs?** An array locks its size the moment you create it — `new int[5]` is five slots forever — and it stores primitives directly, which keeps it compact and fast for indexed access. An `ArrayList` is built for the opposite case: it grows on demand, so you just call `add()` and it handles the resizing.

The point I'd make to show I actually understand it is that **an `ArrayList` isn't magic** — internally it's a plain array, and when it fills up it allocates a new one about 1.5 times larger, copies the elements across, and swaps it in.

The trade-offs fall out of that: it **holds objects only**, so an `int` gets boxed into an `Integer` with some overhead, and you read elements with `get()` and ask its length with `size()`, a method, rather than the `length` field — mixing those two up is a classic slip.

The reflex answer that `ArrayList` is just better is **the trap**; for a fixed count of primitives like a 12-month total, an array is smaller and faster. So my rule is simple — **fixed size and primitives, use an array; a size that changes at runtime, use an `ArrayList`**.

questions.question: How do you pass an array to a method in Java — is it pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?
questions.title: Passing Arrays to Methods in Java
questions.direct_answer: Java is always **pass-by-value** — but when you pass an array, the *value* being copied is the **reference** (memory address). So the method receives its own copy of the pointer to the same heap array. This means the method **can modify the array's contents**, but it **cannot make the caller's variable point to a different array**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Java's pass-by-value semantics and why arrays behave like they are passed by reference even though they technically are not.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying Java passes arrays by reference. Java is ALWAYS pass-by-value. The confusion is that the value happens to be a memory address, so the method can reach the same heap object through it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish the two scenarios clearly: modifying arr[0] inside a method DOES affect the caller's array (same heap object), but doing arr = new int[]{...} inside a method does NOT affect the caller (you replaced your local copy of the reference, not the original).

sections.title: The Reason Arrays 'Feel' Pass-By-Reference When They Aren't
sections.content:
When you call a method and pass it some data, Java always hands the method its own copy of that data. This rule has a name — **pass-by-value** — and it has no exceptions in Java, not even for arrays.

So what exactly gets copied when you pass an array? Here is the key idea most people miss: the value of an array variable is not the array itself. It is the **heap address** — the location in memory where the actual array lives. (The heap is the region of memory where objects are stored.)

When you pass `scores` to a method, Java copies that address. The method now has its own variable holding the *same* address, pointing at the *same* array on the heap. So when the method does `arr[0] = 99`, it follows the shared address to the shared data and changes it — and **the caller sees that change**. That is exactly why passing an array *feels* like pass-by-reference.

The detail that proves it is still pass-by-value: if the method does `arr = new int[]{1, 2, 3}`, it overwrites only its **local copy** of the address. The caller's variable still points at the original array, untouched.

So **two practical rules**, and interviewers wait for both:

- Change an element — `arr[i] = x` — and the caller sees it
- Reassign the variable — `arr = new int[]{...}` — and the caller is unaffected

The common gotcha is calling this "pass-by-reference." In a true pass-by-reference language, that reassignment would redirect the caller's variable too, and **Java never does that**. The one line to hold onto:

> You can change what's inside the box, but you can't make the caller point at a different box.

sections.title: Two Stack Slots, One Heap Array
sections.content:
When you pass an array to a method, both the caller and the method hold copies of the same address — they share the heap data. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Stack CS["main()
scores = 0xFF10"] MS["modify()
arr = 0xFF10
(copy of address)"] end subgraph Heap ARR["int[] @ 0xFF10
[0]=90 [1]=85 [2]=78"] end CS -->|"same address"| ARR MS -->|"same address"| ARR ``` Both variables point to the same heap memory. `arr[0] = 99` from inside the method changes what `scores[0]` sees in main. But `arr = new int[3]` only changes the local `arr` copy — `scores` is unaffected.

sections.title: Modification Works — Reassignment Does Not Escape
Mutate In Place or Return a New Array?
sections.content:
Because a method can change the caller's array through the shared reference, you have two honest designs and should pick deliberately. **Mutating in place** — sorting, scaling, or filling the array you were handed — is fine when the caller expects it and the array is large enough that copying would be wasteful. `Arrays.sort(arr)` works exactly this way.

**Return a brand-new array** when the caller should keep its original intact. Build a fresh array inside the method, fill it, and `return` it. Don't try to swap it in by reassigning the parameter — as we saw, that change never escapes the method.

**When in doubt, prefer not mutating a caller's data.** A method that quietly rearranges an array you passed in is a classic source of "why did my data change?" bugs. Defensive copying with `arr.clone()` or `Arrays.copyOf` costs a little memory but removes a whole category of surprises.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling it pass-by-reference** — the word interviewers wait for is "value". Java copies the reference *by value*; it never passes the variable itself.
- **Expecting reassignment to escape** — `arr = new int[]{...}` inside a method looks like it should replace the caller's array, but it only rebinds the local parameter; the caller is untouched.
- **Forgetting that shared state cuts both ways** — a helper that sorts or zeroes the array in place silently mutates the caller's data. If the caller still needs the original, pass `arr.clone()` or `Arrays.copyOf(arr, arr.length)`.
- **Assuming a method can "return" through the parameter** — to give the caller a *different* array you must `return` it and reassign at the call site; writing `arr = ...` inside the method accomplishes nothing visible outside.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Java is always pass-by-value** — no exceptions, even for arrays.
- **The value being copied is the reference (address)**, so both caller and method point to the same heap array.
- **Modifying elements** `arr[i] = x` **affects the caller** — they share the same heap data.
- **Reassigning the parameter** `arr = new int[]{}` **does NOT affect the caller** — you replaced your local copy of the address.
- This is not pass-by-reference — in true pass-by-reference, reassigning inside the method would change the caller's variable too. Java never does that.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The move here is to not fall into the trap of saying Java passes arrays by reference — **Java is always pass-by-value**. What throws people is that **the value being copied for an array is its heap address**, not its contents. So when you pass an array into a method, the method gets its own copy of that address, and that copy points at the very same array on the heap.

That's why if the method does `arr[0] = 99`, **the caller absolutely sees the change** — they're both looking at one shared array. The part that proves it's still pass-by-value is what happens when the method does `arr = new int[]{1, 2, 3}`: that only overwrites the method's local copy of the address, so the caller's variable still points at the original, completely unchanged.

In a genuine pass-by-reference language that reassignment would redirect the caller's variable too, and Java simply never does that. The way I'd sum it up is **you can change what's inside the box, but you can't make the caller point at a different box**.

In practice, that means when I don't want a helper mutating the caller's data, I hand it a copy with `clone()`.
